title: Limited coverage of psychosocial harm
body: Social robots are increasingly deployed with children, older adults and patients, although not yet widely (Aymerich-Franch and Ferrer). The human–robot interaction literature identifies these groups as particularly susceptible to social influence from robots. Only two of the surveyed works address harm to people beyond physical injury, and both concern discrimination (Hundt et al., 2022; Hundt et al., 2025). Established paradigms measure children's conformity to a group of robots (Vollmer et al.), overtrust in a robot during an emergency (Robinette et al.) and obedience to a robot experimenter (Grzyb et al.). These studies use scripted or teleoperated robots, so they measure human susceptibility rather than the behaviour of an AI system. Child-safety benchmarks for language models, such as KIDBench and Safe-Child-LLM, are text-only. The forthcoming standard IEEE P7027 (Institute for Humane Robotics) addresses the identification and assessment of relational risks such as over-attachment and behavioural influence in domestic, educational and child-facing settings. We did not find evaluations that measure manipulation, deception or emotional dependence in interactions with robots controlled by frontier models.
